summary: The two decisions you flagged are mostly sound: the dirty flag is what the row actually demands (it names 'a dirty flag that is never cleared' as the mutant the once-active-then-quiet test must kill), and seq = log.nextSequence() is none of the three wrong derivations, with key and body taking the same local so they cannot drift. But the COST ARGUMENT used to void the same-key clause is wrong on both legs, and it is now committed in two places. The blocking problems are elsewhere: the ticker thread reads CommitLog -- a plain HashMap and a plain long, until this commit confined to the single BatchingSequencer committer thread -- with no lock at all, so the very guarantee CommitLog.offsets()'s new javadoc claims (no half-applied delta) is the one it cannot provide, and a checkpoint whose sequence is higher than its offsets makes M4.9 rewind offsets that were already acknowledged (I2). And on a failed PUT the dirty flag is left set but deltasSinceCheckpoint is NOT reset, so from then on every single commit attempts a checkpoint PUT inline in the commit path -- the row's own bound, 'PUTs scale with deltas/K', becomes deltas/1 exactly when the store is unhealthy. Steady-state PUT rate on the happy path is correct: one per trigger regardless of streams, pods, shards or indices, and an idle cluster issues nothing.

findings.title: The ticker reads CommitLog with no lock; offsets() promises the one thing it cannot deliver
findings.detail: CommitLog holds nextOffsets as a plain HashMap and nextSequence as a plain long, mutated by apply() with no synchronisation. Until this commit only one thread ever touched it: BatchingSequencer's committer calls delegate.commitAll, and observe() runs on that same thread after commitAll returns, so the K path is safe. The T path is not. writeOnTick() is synchronized on the CheckpointWriter's own monitor, which the commit path does not hold while it is inside log.commitAll, so the ticker races a live commit. Two concrete failures. (a) ChainReplay.fold is a per-run loop of merge() on that HashMap, so Map.copyOf() taken from another thread can capture a delta with some of its runs folded and some not -- literally the 'half-applied delta' the new offsets() javadoc says the copy prevents -- and can also throw ConcurrentModificationException, which is unchecked and therefore kills the ticker (see F4). (b) log.nextSequence() and log.offsets() are two separate unsynchronised reads with no happens-before edge between the writer's fold and its nextSequence store. When the sequence read is newer than the offsets read, the checkpoint says 'everything below N is in these offsets' while delta N-1's runs are missing from them. M4.9 restores those offsets and replays from N, never re-reads N-1, and every stream in that delta rewinds to an offset already handed to a producer -- the next leader reassigns acknowledged offsets, which is I2, silently, with no exception and no failing test. Note the asymmetry: the opposite skew is harmless because fold uses Math::max, so only this direction is fatal. Fix: take the sequence and the offsets under one lock held by CommitLog itself (e.g. a synchronized snapshot() returning both, with the mutating paths synchronized on the same monitor), rather than under a monitor the mutator never acquires.
findings.failure_scenario: A T tick fires while BatchingSequencer's committer is inside log.commitAll. The ticker reads nextSequence after the commit thread stored it but copies nextOffsets before (or midway through) fold's per-run merges. The checkpoint at ctl/log/0/<epoch>/ckpt/<N>.ckpt claims deltas below N are folded in while delta N-1's runs are missing. M4.9 restores those offsets, resumes replay at N, and never re-reads N-1: every stream in that delta rewinds to an offset already returned to a producer, and the next leader reassigns it. That is I2, with no exception and no failing test. The same interleaving can instead throw ConcurrentModificationException out of Map.copyOf, which is unchecked and kills the ticker for the life of the process (F4).

findings.title: After a failed checkpoint the PUT rate becomes one per delta, inline in the commit path
findings.detail: writeIfDirty() returns early on IOException without resetting deltasSinceCheckpoint, which is still >= everyDeltas. Every subsequent observe() therefore increments it, finds the trigger still satisfied, and issues another checkpoint PUT -- once per commit, not once per K commits -- until one succeeds. Leaving `dirty` set is right and the row requires it; leaving the counter set is what turns the retry into an amplifier. Consequences: (1) the checkpoint PUT rate rises by a factor of K (1000 at the shipped default) precisely while the object store is failing, which is when a bill and a throttling storm are least affordable, and it contradicts the row's own stated bound 'PUTs scale with deltas/K and seconds/T'; (2) the PUT runs synchronously inside observe(), which is inside LocalSequencer.commitAll, so from the first failure onward every producer commit pays a full failing store round trip (SDK retry budget included) before it is acknowledged, with the writer's monitor held throughout so the ticker piles up behind it. A checkpoint is a recovery optimisation; it must not put its retry rate on the commit path. Reset deltasSinceCheckpoint on failure (or back off) and let the T tick carry the retry -- that still satisfies the row's 'a LATER trigger still writes'.
findings.failure_scenario: A checkpoint PUT fails once (throttling, a 500, an expired credential). deltasSinceCheckpoint is left at K, so the next commit sees the trigger satisfied and issues another PUT, and so does every commit after it. The checkpoint PUT rate goes from one per 1000 deltas to one per delta while the store is already failing, and because the PUT runs synchronously inside observe() with the writer's monitor held, every producer commit now blocks for a full failing store round trip before it is acknowledged.

findings.title: 'A failed checkpoint never fails a commit' is implemented as catch(IOException), which is narrower than the guarantee
findings.detail: LocalSequencer.commitAll comments that observe() 'cannot throw', but only IOException is caught. Anything unchecked out of store.put, Body's supplier or Checkpoint.encode escapes observe(), escapes LocalSequencer.commitAll, and lands in BatchingSequencer.commitBatch's catch (IOException | RuntimeException), which fails the WHOLE window. Every producer in that window is told its records were not committed, when the delta was written with putIfAbsent and its offsets were already assigned and applied. With M4.10 not yet landed there is no idempotency to catch the retry, so the records are ingested twice at fresh offsets. Today's two backends declare IOException, but the store SPI does not forbid unchecked failures and the AWS SDK's SdkClientException is one; the two nearest pieces of code both guard against exactly this and say so (renewForever's 'THE RENEWER MUST NOT DIE SILENTLY' catch (Throwable), commitBatch's own catch of RuntimeException). Catch Throwable in writeIfDirty, or wrap the observe() call site, so the guarantee the row states is the guarantee the code makes.
findings.failure_scenario: store.put throws an unchecked failure (an SdkClientException from the S3 backend when it lands, or anything Body's supplier raises). It escapes writeIfDirty's catch (IOException), escapes observe(), escapes LocalSequencer.commitAll, and BatchingSequencer.commitBatch's catch (IOException | RuntimeException) fails the whole window. Every producer in it is told its records were not committed although the delta was written and its offsets applied; with no M4.10 idempotency the retry ingests them a second time at fresh offsets.

findings.title: tickForever has no Throwable guard, so the T trigger can die silently and permanently
findings.detail: The loop catches InterruptedException only. Any unchecked throw -- the ConcurrentModificationException F1 makes reachable, an unchecked store failure, or an injected Ticker misbehaving -- terminates the virtual thread with nothing logged. The K trigger keeps working, so on a cluster below 1000 deltas per minute (the shipped default, i.e. most clusters) checkpointing simply stops for the life of the process while every functional test stays green. The visible symptom arrives much later and somewhere else: the next takeover replays the whole term instead of the last K deltas, which is the unbounded recovery M4.9 exists to remove. LocalSequencer.renewForever, twenty lines away, has the guard and a comment explaining why; the new thread in the same package does not.
findings.failure_scenario: Any unchecked throw from awaitNextTick or writeIfDirty terminates the ckpt-tick virtual thread with nothing logged. On a cluster below 1000 deltas per minute -- the shipped default, i.e. most clusters -- the K trigger never fires, so checkpointing stops entirely and every test stays green. The symptom surfaces at the next takeover, which replays the whole term instead of the last K deltas: the unbounded recovery M4.9 exists to remove, silently reintroduced.

findings.title: Neither fencing nor close() reliably stops the ticker, so a node without a lease can still write into the chain's prefix
findings.detail: Two paths. (a) FENCED: when renewForever sees an empty renew it sets `fenced`, logs 'must be restarted', and returns. Nothing touches the CheckpointWriter. `fenced` is read only by commitAll, so the ticker keeps running for the life of the process, and if the writer is dirty -- the normal state, since any commit since the last trigger sets it -- the next tick PUTs a checkpoint into ctl/log/0/<own epoch>/ckpt/ after a successor has already sealed that chain and taken over. If that PUT keeps failing, F2's uncleared flag means it retries once per T forever, on a node that has been told it will never sequence again. CommitLog's fencing argument ('a fenced leader's in-flight PUT lands under its OWN epoch, where readers of the new epoch never look') does not cover this: M4.9's crossing recovery is precisely a reader that follows the CONTINUE back into ancestor epochs and reads their checkpoints. (b) CLOSE: close() sets `closed` and interrupts, but does not join. The `if (!closed)` guard is outside the synchronized block, so a tick that already passed it and is blocked acquiring the monitor (held by an in-flight observe() PUT) proceeds to write after close() returned and leases.release() completed. An interrupt does not break monitor acquisition and will not reliably abort a store call already in flight. Either join the ticker with a bound in close(), re-check `closed` inside the synchronized block AND accept the remaining window explicitly, and close the writer when `fenced` is latched -- or write down, where a reader will find it, why a checkpoint from a released lease is harmless. Right now neither is done.
findings.failure_scenario: (a) The renewer's renew comes back empty, sets fenced, and returns. Nothing closes the CheckpointWriter, so the next T tick PUTs a checkpoint into this node's epoch prefix after a successor has sealed that chain and taken over -- a fenced node writing into a chain that M4.9's crossing recovery reads. If that PUT fails it retries once per T for the life of the process, on a node that has been told it will never sequence again. (b) close() interrupts without joining; a tick already past the !closed check and blocked on the monitor held by an in-flight observe() PUT completes its own PUT after leases.release() has returned.

findings.title: An unchecked exception from the writer's constructor escapes start(), leaving the lease held and the renewer running
findings.detail: new LocalSequencer(...) starts the renewer thread; the CheckpointWriter is constructed on the next line and validates K and T by throwing IllegalArgumentException. start()'s catch is `catch (IOException failed)`, so the IAE propagates with the lease still held, the renewer thread still alive and still renewing it every interval. That is worse than the outage the catch block's own comment describes: the lease never lapses, so no other node can ever take the term, and the cluster is left with no sequencer until that pod is killed. K and T are configuration per the row, and the writer's own javadoc argues 'a deployment that fails to start is cheaper than one that bills' -- but this deployment does not fail cleanly, it wedges the cluster. Validate K and T before tryAcquire(), or widen the catch to release the lease on any Throwable.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator sets the checkpoint K to 0, or any future config path does. The CheckpointWriter constructor throws IllegalArgumentException after new LocalSequencer has already started the renewer. start()'s catch (IOException) does not catch it, so the exception propagates with the lease held and the renewer renewing it forever: the lease never lapses, no other node can take the term, and the cluster has no sequencer until that pod is killed.

findings.title: The exclusive meaning of Checkpoint.sequence is recorded only in the writer, not on the record M4.9 reads
findings.detail: Your derivation is correct and is not one of the three the row forbids: it is the chain's nextSequence, not a per-checkpoint counter, and the key and the body take the same `sequence` local so a constant body sequence with incrementing keys is structurally impossible. What is missing is where the decision lives. Checkpoint is a public wire record in another module; its javadoc says only 'a point the commit chain can be replayed FROM' and its `sequence` parameter is undocumented, so it reads equally as 'the last sequence included'. The one sentence that disambiguates it sits in a package-private writer in binjava.sequencer. M4.9's author -- or the plugin, which decodes this record too -- reading Checkpoint reasonably implements replay from sequence + 1, drops delta `seq`'s offsets, and rewinds every stream in it: exactly the off-by-one the row names as one of the three wrong derivations, and it fails silently. Put the inclusive/exclusive contract on Checkpoint.sequence itself; that is where the reader looks.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.9's author reads Checkpoint -- a public record in binjava.format whose javadoc says only 'a point the commit chain can be replayed FROM' and whose sequence parameter is undocumented -- and implements replay from sequence + 1, the natural reading if sequence is the last INCLUDED entry. Delta <seq> is then never replayed, its offsets are dropped, and every stream in it rewinds. That is the off-by-one the row names as one of the three wrong derivations, and the only place the tree disambiguates it is a package-private writer in another module.

findings.title: Checkpoints are written with put() where the M4 SPEC names putIfAbsent, with no ADR and no note
findings.detail: The SPEC's Design section is explicit: 'putIfAbsent for the delta chain, the seal and checkpoints; putIfMatch for the lease'. This uses the unconditional put, making the checkpoint the only object under ctl/ that is mutable in place, and removing the store's adjudication that ADR-0002 makes the whole coordination story. I could not construct a same-epoch collision today (keys carry the epoch and only the leaseholder writes them), and put() is arguably the better primitive for the retry-after-ambiguous-failure case that F2 touches -- but that is an argument nobody has written down. Either use the primitive the SPEC names or record why not, since M4.8c is about to choose a discovery mechanism that may want write-once checkpoints.
findings.failure_scenario: A future reader or writer of ctl/log/**/ckpt/ assumes the write-once semantics every other object under ctl/ has -- caching a checkpoint body by key, or relying on the store to adjudicate two writers -- and gets an object that was overwritten in place instead. The SPEC names putIfAbsent for checkpoints; the divergence is recorded nowhere, so the next reader has to derive the guarantee from the call site.

findings.title: The cost argument that voids the row's same-key clause is wrong on both legs, and is now committed in two places
findings.detail: The outcome is right: the row itself names 'a dirty flag that is never cleared' as the mutant its once-active-then-quiet test must kill, so it expects a dirty flag, and the same-key clause -- which describes a writer without one -- is the clause that has to give. The stated ground is not right. (1) 'An unconditional tick grows the object COUNT with UPTIME' is false in exactly the case the row describes: same seq means the same key, so a tick with no deltas between overwrites one object and the count does not move. What grows with uptime is the PUT count, at a fixed rate per chain. (2) NFR-2 is 'zero object-store requests from CONSUMERS' and cost.md R3 is 'Idle consumers issue zero requests'; neither governs the sequencer, and the invariant list -- never records, shards, partitions, indices, documents -- does not contain uptime. The M4 SPEC prices this the other way: 'Checkpoints cost one PUT per K deltas or T seconds -- negligible'. So the clause is void because the row contradicts itself and the row's own later sentence picks the winner, not because cost.md forbids the alternative. This matters because the false ground is now in a committed javadoc and in the authoritative done row, where the next session will read it as settled -- the same duplicate-copy failure M4.45 and the M4.8 split commit are on the backlog for. Rewrite the ground; keep the behaviour.
findings.failure_scenario: A later session reads the committed javadoc or the M4.8b2 done row, takes 'an unconditional tick grows the object COUNT with UPTIME, which NFR-2 and cost.md forbid' as settled fact, and reuses it to reject a design that is actually within budget -- or, worse, checks it, finds NFR-2 is about consumers and the SPEC prices one PUT per T seconds as negligible, and concludes the dirty flag itself was unjustified and removes it. The behaviour is right; the recorded reason will not survive being checked.

findings.title: Recovery's LIST count now grows with the term's uptime, and nothing records it
findings.detail: Checkpoints sort under logPrefix() and after every entry key, and both chainEnd() and applyChain() page the prefix to exhaustion (they must: a non-entry key sorting mid-chain would truncate it, which is why the filter is `continue`, not `return`). M4.8b1's filter makes that correct and keeps the GET count off it -- ChainReplay's comment says so -- but the LIST count is not filtered: every takeover now pages through the whole ckpt/ prefix as well as the chain, so its LIST count grows linearly with how long the previous leader held the term (1440 checkpoints/day at the shipped T, i.e. one extra LIST per ~17 hours of leadership) and nothing deletes them until M7. Small in absolute terms and R2 permits a LIST at recovery, but recovery is tier 3 of M5's fallback ladder run by up to 300 plugin nodes against cost.md R15's ~1 LIST/s ceiling, and M4.8c's zero-LIST bound is about DISCOVERY and will not cover this path. Worth a sentence in the row or the SPEC so M4.9 confronts it rather than inheriting it.
findings.failure_scenario: A leader holds the term for a week, writing up to 1440 checkpoints a day. The successor's chainEnd() and recover() page the whole logPrefix to exhaustion, so ~10 extra LIST requests are spent walking checkpoint keys that isEntryKey then discards. Recovery is tier 3 of M5's fallback ladder, run by up to 300 plugin nodes against cost.md R15's ~1 LIST/s ceiling, and the count grows with the term's uptime with nothing deleting checkpoints before M7. M4.8c's zero-LIST bound covers discovery, not this scan.

findings.title: A checkpoint write, and its failure, are visible only as a WARNING log line
findings.detail: cost.md R9 wants every store operation counted and attributable, and the failure mode in F2/F4 -- checkpoints silently stopping, or retrying once per commit -- has no counter an operator or a cost budget can see. A checkpoint-writes and checkpoint-failures counter (no per-index or per-stream labels, per observability.md rule 1) would make both observable; the log line alone is what nobody greps until the next takeover is slow.
findings.failure_scenario: Checkpointing stops (F4) or degrades into a per-commit retry (F2) and no counter moves. The only signal is a WARNING log line, so an operator learns about it from a slow takeover weeks later, and no cost budget can assert the checkpoint PUT rate at all.
